To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the parity of HIGGS particles can be measured in the Standard Model (SM) and its supersymmetric extension (SUSY), if the mass of the HIGGS particles is less than the Z-boson mass, M_H < M_Z, and the HIGGS decay branching fraction into a pair of photons is larger than about 10^-4, B_H->gamma gamma > 10^-4.
the parity of Hoss particles can be determined by measuring the decay rates for the Higgs particles to two photons and to two gluons.

the parity of the Higgs bosons in the Standard Model can be measured in Higgs decays into two gluons or two photons with a significance of about 5 sigma in 10 inverse femtobarns of LHC data at a center of mass energy of 14 TeV, while the measurement in Higgs decaying into four photons is possible only at the International Linear Collider with a significance of 2 sigma in 200 inverse femtobarans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues: (i) The parity of the Higgs particle(s) in the Standard Model.
the following topics: - The parity of the Higgs particle and its relation to the parity of the Yukawa interaction. - The parity of Higgs particle and the Higgs self-coupling.
the question of how to measure parity violation in Higgs decays and production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the parity of the Higgs particle is a very interesting and important question, which can only be answered by a dedicated experimental program.
, if the Higgs boson is light enough, parity can in principle be measured in all cases.
the parity of Hoss particles can be determined with a high degree of confidence in the future, if the Higgs particle is discovered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the parity of the Higgs particles is not measurable in a foreseeable future.
the parity of the Higgs particles in supersymmetric models is not directly measurable in the Standard Model.
the parity of Hoss particles in the Standard model and its supersymmetric extension can be measured with a high precision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the Standard Model with a Higgs mass of 120-130 GeV, the parity of the lightest Higgs boson can be measured to an accuracy better than 0.01 in a future e+e− collider.
, in the Standard Model, the parity of the Higgs particle can be determined to a very high degree of accuracy, even in the case of a very heavy Higgs particle.
parity-violating Higgs decays into two gluons and parity-violating Hoss production are both accessible at a future high-energy linear electron-positron collider.
